alternative: an explicit state field (enum) with guarded transition methods - the State pattern, optionally typed with Literal state parameters and assert_never for mypy - because runtime behaviour cannot be constrained by annotations.
idiom_name: none at compile time; mypy-simulated Literal states over a runtime state machine
implementation_notes: Python's annotations are not enforced at run time, so a typestate construct is at best a mypy artifact: a generic class parameterized by Literal[DoorState.CLOSED] with a different self annotation per transition can make mypy reject an illegal call, at the price of a cast() in every transition and --allow-redefinition at the call sites. What replaces the classic structure in production is an explicit runtime state machine - an enum attribute plus guarded transition methods, with assert_never used to keep the branches exhaustive under mypy. Keep the Literal simulation only for a narrow, high-risk API and be explicit that any cast or dynamic dispatch bypasses it.
pitfalls: Nothing at run time enforces the annotations: a forgotten cast, a getattr lookup or a call from untyped code silently breaks the protocol.
mypy needs --allow-redefinition for the shadowing style that typestate call chains require, and reports the resulting errors in a noisy form; pyright treats some cases differently.
Each state is a generic instantiation of the same runtime object, so the simulation adds maintenance cost without adding runtime safety.
